intro: The Talmud is full of stories and big ideas, but much of it is about daily life. This unit reads famous passages in paraphrase. You will see the Talmud ask what time it is, how Shabbat works, how to light Hanukkah candles, and who pays when an ox falls into a pit.

Two threads run through every passage. The first is argument: a question, a proof, an objection and an answer. The second is mercy: each ruling protects someone, such as a worker, a finder, a neighbor, or a person who might be shamed. Watch for both as you read.

By the end, you will be able to explain what a sugya is and follow its moves. You will be able to name the tractate and page of a famous passage. You will be able to say what a ruling protects and how different Jewish readers have read it.
bigQuestion: How does the Talmud turn questions about time and harm into lessons about living with other people?

title: Sugyot in Paraphrase I: Time and Damages

chapters.title: Shabbat, the Shema and Hanukkah
chapters.bigQuestion: Why does the Talmud begin by asking what time it is, and what does that first question show about how it thinks?

story.title: The First Page Asks the Time
story.kicker: Two study partners open the very first page of the Talmud and find a question about the evening sky.
paragraphs: It is a Tuesday evening in a living room on the North Side of Chicago. Two study partners, a retired nurse and a high school junior, have a large book open between them. It is the first volume of the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Berakhot. They are part of a Daf Yomi group, people around the world who read one page a day. Today is page 2a, the very first page. The junior leans in. "So what does it start with? Creation? God?" The nurse smiles. "It starts with a question about the time."

The Mishnah's first line asks: from when may a person recite the evening Shema? The Shema is the short passage from Deuteronomy that Jewish tradition recites twice a day. The Mishnah answers with a picture, not a clock. From the hour the priests come in to eat their holy food. Then it gives three views on how late is too late. Rabbi Eliezer says the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until dawn.

The junior frowns. "Why not just say sunset?" The nurse points to the next lines. "That is what the Gemara asks, more or less." The Gemara, the commentary that surrounds the Mishnah on the page, begins with its own puzzle. Where does this teacher stand? Why does he start with the evening instead of the morning? And who said there was a duty to recite the Shema at all? The answer comes from a verse: you shall speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up.

An hour later they have read two paragraphs. They have met priests, stars, a poor man eating bread with salt, and King David's harp, which tradition says woke him at midnight. The junior closes the book. "That is a lot for one question." The nurse nods. "That is the whole Talmud. One question, argued with care. Tomorrow we do page 2b."
story.think: Why might a book about law and life begin with a question about time instead of a question about belief?

lessons.title: From When Do We Recite?
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah opens with a question about the earliest time to say the evening Shema, and answers it with a picture of priests eating.
reading: The Talmud is a long work, but it begins with one short line. The *Mishnah* of Berakhot 1:1 asks: from when do we recite the *Shema* in the evening? The Shema is a set of Bible verses, beginning with Deuteronomy 6:4, that Jewish tradition recites each morning and evening. Berakhot means "blessings." It is the first tractate, or book, of the Talmud, and it is about prayer.

The Mishnah does not answer with a clock time. It says: from the hour the priests enter to eat their *terumah*. Terumah was a portion of the harvest given to priests in ancient Israel. A priest who had become ritually unclean had to wait until nightfall to eat it. So "when the priests enter to eat" is a way of saying "when the stars come out." The rule is told through a scene people knew.

Then the Mishnah asks how late a person may recite. It gives three answers. Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says until dawn. The Mishnah keeps all three views on the page. That is a habit the whole Talmud follows: it records disagreement instead of erasing it.

words.d: the short, first layer of the Talmud, a code of Jewish law edited c. 200 CE
Bible verses beginning with Deuteronomy 6:4 that Jewish tradition recites morning and evening
a share of the harvest given to priests in ancient Israel; eaten only in a state of ritual purity

look.title: The Mishnah's First Line
look.text: From when may the Shema be recited in the evening? From the hour the priests enter to eat their terumah, until the end of the first watch; these are the words of Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages say: until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: until the dawn comes up.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1, paraphrased from the Hebrew; compare Rodkinson's translation (1896–1903)
look.prompt: Three answers are given for the latest time. Which one gives a person the most time, and which the least?

check.q: What does the tractate name Berakhot mean?
check.why: Berakhot means "blessings." It is the first tractate of the Talmud and deals with prayer.

check.q: How does the Mishnah describe the earliest time for the evening Shema?
choices: when the priests enter to eat their terumah
check.why: The Mishnah uses a scene, priests entering to eat terumah at nightfall, instead of a clock time.

check.q: Who says the Shema may be recited until dawn?
check.why: Rabban Gamliel gives the latest time, dawn. Rabbi Eliezer says the first watch and the Sages say midnight.

lessons.title: Where Does the Teacher Stand?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara's first move is to ask what the Mishnah assumes, and it finds the answer in a verse from Deuteronomy.
reading: The *Gemara* is the discussion that surrounds the Mishnah on the Talmud page. It was built up by teachers called *amoraim* over about three centuries. On Berakhot 2a the Gemara begins with a sharp question. The Mishnah asked "from when." But it never said that a person must recite the Shema at all. Where does this teacher stand? In other words, what is he assuming?

The Gemara answers: the teacher stands on a verse. Deuteronomy 6:7 says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Rabbinic tradition reads that as the evening and morning Shema. So the Mishnah does not need to say there is a duty. It takes the verse as known and asks the next question, the time.

Then the Gemara asks a second question. Why start with the evening and not the morning? One answer points back to the verse, which puts lying down first. Another answer points to the story of creation. Genesis 1:5 says "there was evening and there was morning, one day." In Jewish tradition the day begins at nightfall. The Talmud's first page is already doing what it will do everywhere: asking why, and proving from a text.

words.d: the discussion of the Mishnah that fills the Talmud page, built up by the amoraim c. 200–500 CE
the teachers of the Gemara in the land of Israel and Babylonia, c. 200–500 CE

look.title: The Verse Behind the Question
look.text: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
look.prompt: Which words in this verse does the Gemara use to explain an evening and a morning Shema?

check.q: What is the Gemara's first question on Berakhot 2a?
choices: Why is the Shema in Hebrew?
Which prayer comes after the Shema?
What does the Mishnah assume when it asks "from when"?
check.why: The Gemara asks "where does the teacher stand," meaning what the Mishnah takes for granted.

check.q: Which verse does the Gemara say the duty to recite the Shema rests on?
check.why: Deuteronomy 6:7 speaks of "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up," read as evening and morning.

check.q: Why does one answer say the evening Shema is discussed first?
choices: because the Temple opened at night
because in Jewish tradition the day begins at evening, as in Genesis 1:5
because the morning Shema is optional
check.why: The Gemara cites Genesis 1:5, "there was evening and there was morning," for the day beginning at nightfall.

lessons.title: Three Ways to See Night
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara compares several teachings that mark nightfall by priests, by stars and by a poor man's supper, and asks whether they agree.
reading: How do you know when night has come? The Gemara on Berakhot 2a–2b collects several answers from early teachings called *baraitot*. A baraita is a teaching from the age of the Mishnah that was not put into the Mishnah itself. One baraita marks nightfall by the priests going in to eat terumah. Another marks it by the stars coming out. Another marks it by the hour a poor man sits down to his bread with salt.

The Gemara treats these like witnesses in a case. Do they say the same thing, or do they clash? If the poor man eats before the priests, then the two markers give different times. The Gemara tests each pairing. It brings a verse from Nehemiah 4 about workers who labored from dawn until the stars came out, to show that "stars" means night in the Bible too.

Notice what the Gemara is doing. It is not settling for one answer. It is lining up sources, checking one against another and asking which can stand together. This move, question, proof, objection, answer, is called a *sugya*, a unit of Talmudic argument. The first sugya of the Talmud is about a sky turning dark and a poor man's supper.

words.d: a teaching from the age of the Mishnah that was left out of the Mishnah but quoted in the Gemara
one unit of Talmudic argument on a single question: question, proof, objection, answer

look.title: Three Markers, One Moment
look.text: Marker A: the priests, who waited all day, go in to eat their terumah. Marker B: three stars can be seen in the sky. Marker C: a poor man, home from work, sits down to bread and salt. The Gemara asks whether A, B and C happen at the same time.
look.prompt: Which marker would be easiest for an ordinary person to check in a village with no clocks? Why might the Gemara want more than one?

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: a teaching from the Mishnah's age that the Mishnah left out
check.why: A baraita is an early teaching not included in the Mishnah but quoted by the Gemara.

check.q: Which of these is NOT one of the nightfall markers the Gemara discusses?
choices: the priests entering to eat terumah
check.why: The three markers are priests, stars and the poor man's meal. There is no bell.

check.q: What does the Gemara do with the several teachings about nightfall?
choices: checks whether they agree with one another
throws out the ones about poor people
check.why: The Gemara lines up the sources and tests whether each pair can stand together, the basic move of a sugya.

lessons.title: Forty Less One
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah lists thirty-nine main categories of work that Jewish law forbids on Shabbat, from sowing to carrying.
reading: The Bible says to rest on the seventh day, *Shabbat*, but it does not give a full list of what "work" means. Tractate Shabbat, the Talmud's book about the day of rest, fills that gap. Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists the main categories of forbidden labor. It calls them "forty less one," that is, thirty-nine.

The list reads like a tour of ancient life. It begins with the steps of making bread: sowing, plowing, reaping, binding sheaves, threshing, winnowing, sorting, grinding, sifting, kneading, baking. Then come the steps of making cloth: shearing wool, washing it, combing it, dyeing, spinning, weaving and more. Then come working with hides, writing and erasing, building and tearing down, lighting and putting out a fire, and one last item: carrying from one domain to another.

Each of the thirty-nine is called an *av melakhah*, a "father" or main category. Related actions are its "children." Grinding wheat is a father; the Talmud asks what else counts as grinding. Jewish communities differ on how the list applies to modern life. Orthodox practice treats the list as binding and works out cases like electricity. Reform Judaism leaves much of this to personal choice. Conservative Judaism has ruled on some cases, such as driving to synagogue, in its own way.

words.d: the seventh day, from Friday sunset to Saturday night, kept as a day of rest in Jewish tradition
one of the thirty-nine main categories of work forbidden on Shabbat in Mishnah Shabbat 7:2

look.title: How the Thirty-Nine Group Up
look.cite: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2, grouped as the Talmud's readers commonly group them
look.prompt: Add the rows. Which two groups make up more than half of the list, and what does that say about the world the list came from?

check.q: How many main categories of Shabbat work does Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 list?
check.why: The Mishnah says "forty less one," which is thirty-nine.

check.q: What is an av melakhah?
choices: a main category of forbidden Shabbat work
a blessing said on Friday night
check.why: Av melakhah means a "father" category; related actions are counted under it.

check.q: Which of these is the LAST item in the Mishnah's list?
choices: carrying from one domain to another
check.why: The list ends with carrying from one domain to another, which later became the subject of the eruv.

lessons.title: Why the Tabernacle?
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud explains the thirty-nine labors as the kinds of work used to build the tabernacle in the wilderness.
reading: Where does the list of thirty-nine come from? The Bible does not print it. The Gemara in Shabbat 49b gives an answer from the age of the amoraim. Rabbi Chanina bar Chama teaches that the categories match the labors used to build the *tabernacle*, the portable sanctuary the Israelites carried through the wilderness in the book of Exodus. Sowing and reaping grew plants for dyes. Shearing, spinning and weaving made the curtains. Writing marked the boards.

Why connect the two? In Exodus 35, Moses tells the people about Shabbat and then, in the very next lines, about building the tabernacle. Rabbinic readers took that order as a hint. The work that was holy enough to build the sanctuary is the work that stops on the holy day. Another teacher in the Gemara counts the word "labor" in the Torah and finds it thirty-nine times. The Talmud keeps both explanations.

Historians describe this list as the rabbis' way of turning a broad command into something a person could actually keep. Jewish readers across the centuries have called the tabernacle link a beautiful idea: rest mirrors the building of a holy place. Either way, the lesson for a student of the Talmud is the method. A number appears in the Mishnah; the Gemara asks where it came from; the answer is found in the Torah's own arrangement.

words.d: the portable sanctuary the Israelites built in the wilderness, described in Exodus; in Hebrew, mishkan
the second book of the Torah, which tells of leaving Egypt, the Ten Commandments and the tabernacle

look.title: The Command to Rest
look.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
look.prompt: This verse says to keep the day holy but does not list what to stop doing. Where does the Talmud say the list of thirty-nine comes from?

check.q: According to Shabbat 49b, what do the thirty-nine labors match?
choices: the work used to build the tabernacle
check.why: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama teaches that the categories correspond to the labors of building the tabernacle.

check.q: What hint does the Talmud find in Exodus 35?
choices: Shabbat and the tabernacle are described one right after the other
the tabernacle was built on Shabbat
check.why: The passage on Shabbat sits right next to the passage on building the tabernacle, and rabbinic readers connected them.

check.q: How did the Gemara handle two different explanations for the number thirty-nine?
check.why: The Talmud keeps both the tabernacle explanation and the word-count explanation side by side.

lessons.title: Carrying and the Eruv
lessons.mainIdea: Carrying between a private and a public space is one of the thirty-nine labors, and the eruv is the rabbis' way of making a shared space count as one home.
reading: The very first Mishnah of tractate Shabbat is about carrying, not cooking or lighting. It pictures a poor man standing in the street and a homeowner standing inside his door. If one reaches in and takes an object from the other's hand, who has "carried"? The Mishnah works through the cases. Carrying from a private *domain*, like a house, to a public one, like a street, is the thirty-ninth labor.

This rule creates a problem for a family. Can a parent carry a baby to a neighbor's home on Shabbat? Can someone bring food to a courtyard shared by many houses? The rabbis of the Mishnah developed the *eruv*. The word means "mixing" or "joining." Households in a shared courtyard put a little food in one place before Shabbat. That act joins them into a single household for the day, so they may carry within the shared space. A whole tractate, Eruvin, is about this.

Today a community eruv is often a thin wire or string on poles that marks the edge of an area, with the food set aside in one place. Many Orthodox communities keep one; Chicago has eruvin in several neighborhoods. Some Jewish readers see the eruv as a clever act of mercy that keeps the law and keeps families together. Others, inside and outside Judaism, see it as a legal fiction. The Talmud itself shows the rabbis arguing over its limits in detail.

words.d: a kind of space in Shabbat law, such as a private home or a public street
a joining of households or areas, set up before Shabbat, that allows carrying within a shared space

look.title: The Poor Man and the Homeowner
look.text: A poor man stands in the street. A homeowner stands inside his doorway. Case one: the poor man reaches his hand inside and puts a loaf in the homeowner's hand. Case two: the homeowner reaches out and puts a loaf in the poor man's hand. Mishnah Shabbat 1:1 asks, in each case, who moved the loaf from one domain to another.
look.prompt: In each case, whose hand crossed the doorway? Why would the Mishnah care about the difference?

check.q: What does the first Mishnah of tractate Shabbat discuss?
choices: carrying between a house and a street
check.why: Mishnah Shabbat 1:1 pictures a poor man and a homeowner passing an object across a doorway.

check.q: What does the word eruv mean?
check.why: Eruv means "joining" or "mixing"; households are joined into one for the day.

check.q: Which tractate is devoted to the eruv?
check.why: Tractate Eruvin deals with joining domains so that carrying is allowed on Shabbat.

lessons.title: What Is Hanukkah?
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells the story of one jar of oil that burned eight days, while the books of Maccabees tell of the same festival without the oil.
reading: Hanukkah is not in the Hebrew Bible. So the Gemara in Shabbat 21b, in the middle of a discussion about oil and wicks, stops and asks: what is *Hanukkah*? Its answer is a baraita. In the days of the Greeks, the Greeks entered the sanctuary and made all its oil unfit. When the *Hasmoneans*, the priestly family who led the revolt, won and entered the Temple, they searched and found one small jar of oil still sealed by the High Priest. It held enough for one day. A miracle happened, the baraita says, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year those days were fixed as a festival of praise and thanks.

Historians date the events to about 164 BCE, when Judah Maccabee's forces rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem. The word Hanukkah means "dedication." The books of 1 and 2 Maccabees, written closer to the events, describe an eight-day celebration of the rededication. They do not mention the jar of oil. The oil story appears in rabbinic sources.

Readers handle the gap in different ways. Traditional Jewish readers accept the Talmud's account as history preserved by the rabbis. Many academic readers see the oil story as a later teaching that shifted the holiday's meaning from a military victory to a quiet miracle. The Talmud itself is not very interested in the battles. It asks what Hanukkah is and answers with a lamp.

words.d: the eight-day festival of lights marking the rededication of the Temple, c. 164 BCE; the word means "dedication"
the priestly family, including Judah Maccabee, who led the revolt against Greek rule in Judea
two ancient books, 1 and 2 Maccabees, that tell of the revolt and the Temple's rededication

look.title: The Talmud's Hanukkah Story
look.text: What is Hanukkah? The sages taught: when the Greeks entered the sanctuary they made all the oils there unfit. When the Hasmonean house grew strong and defeated them, they searched and found only one jar of oil that still bore the seal of the High Priest, with enough to light for one day. A miracle happened, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year they fixed these days as a festival with praise and thanksgiving.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b, paraphrased from the Aramaic and Hebrew
look.prompt: What does this account leave out that 1 Maccabees includes, and what does it include that 1 Maccabees does not?

check.q: Where in the Talmud is the story of the oil found?
check.why: The Gemara in Shabbat 21b asks "What is Hanukkah?" and answers with the baraita about the oil.

check.q: What do the books of Maccabees describe that differs from the Talmud's account?
choices: an eight-day rededication with no jar of oil
check.why: 1 and 2 Maccabees tell of an eight-day celebration of the Temple's rededication but do not mention the oil.

check.q: What does the word Hanukkah mean?
check.why: Hanukkah means "dedication," for the rededication of the Temple c. 164 BCE.

lessons.title: Hillel and Shammai on the Lights
lessons.mainIdea: The House of Shammai lights eight candles the first night and fewer each night; the House of Hillel starts with one and adds, because holiness should grow.
reading: The same page, Shabbat 21b, records a famous disagreement. The basic duty, the Gemara says, is one lamp for each household each night. Those who do more light one for each person. And those who do the most? Here the two great schools of the first century BCE and first century CE part ways. The *House of Shammai* says: on the first night light eight, and go down one each night. The *House of Hillel* says: on the first night light one, and go up one each night.

The Gemara gives reasons for both. For Shammai's school, the number matches the days still to come; it is also like the bulls offered on the festival of Sukkot, which decrease each day. For Hillel's school, the number matches the days already passed, and there is a rule: in matters of holiness we go up, not down.

Notice how the Talmud treats the losing side. It does not call the House of Shammai wrong. It explains their logic with care and keeps it on the page. Jewish tradition holds that in most disputes the law follows Hillel's school. But a student who reads only Hillel's view has read half the page.

words.d: the school of the sage Hillel; in most disputes rabbinic tradition follows its rulings
the school of the sage Shammai, usually stricter, whose views the Talmud records alongside Hillel's

look.title: Candles Each Night, Hillel's Way
look.unit: lights, not counting the helper candle
look.cite: Shabbat 21b, the view of the House of Hillel
look.prompt: How many lights would the House of Shammai set out on each night? Do both schools use the same total number over eight nights?

check.q: How does the House of Shammai say to light the Hanukkah lamps?
choices: one the first night, adding one each night
eight the first night, one fewer each night
check.why: The House of Shammai begins with eight and decreases, matching the days still to come.

check.q: What rule does the Gemara give for the House of Hillel's view?
choices: in matters of holiness we go up, not down
the number should match the bulls of Sukkot
check.why: The Gemara explains Hillel's school by the rule that we increase in holiness and do not decrease.

check.q: According to the Gemara, what is the basic duty of Hanukkah lighting?
choices: one lamp for the whole town
one lamp for each household each night
check.why: The basic duty is one lamp per household; extra lamps are for those who do more.

lessons.title: We Light Like Hillel
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish practice follows the House of Hillel and places the lamp where passersby can see it, because the point is to make the miracle known.
reading: Jewish communities today light the way the House of Hillel taught: one flame the first night, eight on the last. Adding the helper candle, the *shamash*, which lights the others, a family uses forty-four candles over the holiday. Ashkenazi and Sephardi customs differ on small points, such as whether each person in a home lights a separate lamp. The rule to increase each night is shared.

Shabbat 21b also asks where and when to light. The lamp is placed at the door facing the street, or, for someone upstairs, in a window. The Gemara gives the reason in two words: *pirsumei nisa*, making the miracle known. The lighting is a public act, meant to be seen. The time is from sunset until the last foot leaves the market, that is, while people are still passing by.

Then the Gemara adds a note of mercy. In a time of danger, when it was not safe to show a Jewish lamp outside, a person may set it on the table indoors, and that is enough. The law bends to protect the life of the one keeping it. Many Chicago homes and public squares light large menorahs each December; the practice on the street goes back to this page.

words.d: the helper candle used to light the other Hanukkah lights
"making the miracle known," the Talmud's reason for placing the Hanukkah lamp where people can see it

look.title: Where Should the Lamp Go?
look.text: Case one: a family in a house with a door onto a busy street. Case two: a family living on the third floor. Case three: a family in a town where showing a Jewish lamp outside would bring harm. Shabbat 21b gives a different placement for each.
look.prompt: Match each case to its placement: the doorway, the window, or the table. What single goal explains the first two, and what different goal explains the third?

check.q: Which school's practice do Jewish communities follow for Hanukkah lights today?
check.why: Practice follows the House of Hillel: one light the first night, increasing to eight.

check.q: What does pirsumei nisa mean?
check.why: Pirsumei nisa means publicizing the miracle, the reason the lamp faces the street.

check.q: What does the Gemara allow in a time of danger?
choices: placing the lamp on the table indoors
lighting only on the eighth night
check.why: In danger a person may set the lamp on the table inside, and that fulfills the duty.

lessons.title: The Sons Who Came Home Late
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah's first page shows a strict rule, midnight, made not to punish but to keep people from putting things off.
reading: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 ends with a small story. Rabban Gamliel's sons came home from a wedding feast after midnight. They had not yet recited the evening Shema. They asked their father whether it was too late. He told them: if the dawn has not come up, you must recite. His own view was that the duty lasts until dawn.

Then he explained the Sages, who had said midnight. They did not mean that the duty ends at midnight, he says. They set the earlier time to keep a person far from wrongdoing. If people think they have until dawn, they may fall asleep and miss it. Midnight is a fence built around the real limit.

This idea of a *fence* around the law appears across the Talmud. A rule is set earlier or stricter than the Torah requires, so that people do not slip. Readers see two things in Rabban Gamliel's answer. One is the argument: he explains a rival view rather than mocking it. The other is mercy: he tells tired young men who came home late that they have not failed. The first page of the Talmud holds both.

words.d: in rabbinic tradition, a rule set stricter than the Torah's own limit, to keep people from crossing it
a leading sage of the Mishnah's age; in Berakhot 1:1 he tells his sons the Shema may be said until dawn

look.title: How Late Is Too Late?
rows: Rabbi Eliezer: end of the first watch
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1; a night counted as twelve hours with three watches, as the Gemara discusses
look.prompt: Rabban Gamliel says the Sages agree with him on the real limit. Then why would they teach a six-hour rule instead of a twelve-hour one?

check.q: What did Rabban Gamliel tell his sons who came home after midnight?
choices: they must recite it, since dawn had not come
they should wait for the morning Shema
check.why: Rabban Gamliel held that the duty lasts until dawn, so the sons still had to recite.

check.q: Why, according to Rabban Gamliel, did the Sages say midnight?
choices: because Rabbi Eliezer asked them to
to keep people from putting it off and missing it
because the stars set at midnight
check.why: The Sages' midnight limit is a fence, set early so people would not fall asleep and miss the Shema.

check.q: What is a fence around the law?
choices: a rule set stricter than the Torah's limit so people do not cross it
check.why: A fence is a stricter rule made to protect the real limit, a common idea in rabbinic tradition.

lessons.title: Time Is the First Subject
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud opens with time because Jewish law, as the rabbis shaped it, turns ordinary hours into a pattern of duties and rest.
reading: Why does a work about all of Jewish life open with clocks and calendars? Look at the order. The first tractate, Berakhot, asks when to pray. The second order of the Mishnah, called Moed or "appointed times," is entirely about Shabbat and the holidays. Hanukkah's rules appear inside Shabbat, because the question was about oil that may be used for lamps on Shabbat.

Time in the Talmud is measured by the world, not by machines. Nightfall is when stars appear. The day starts at evening, following Genesis 1:5. Hours are twelfths of daylight, so a winter hour is shorter than a summer hour. The Shema, Shabbat and Hanukkah each take a slice of ordinary time and give it a shape.

Different readers explain this differently. Many religious readers say time is the first subject because holiness in Judaism lives in when, not only in where; after the Temple was destroyed, sacred time replaced sacred space. Academic readers point out that the Mishnah's editors simply began with daily practice, the Shema and blessings, before moving to the farm and the festivals. Both readings agree on the fact: the Talmud begins by asking what time it is.

words.d: "appointed times," the second of the six orders of the Mishnah, covering Shabbat and the festivals
one of the six large divisions of the Mishnah; each order holds several tractates

look.title: Evening First
look.text: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.
look.prompt: Which comes first in this verse, evening or morning? How does the Gemara on Berakhot 2a use that order?

check.q: What is the order Moed about?
check.why: Moed means "appointed times"; it is the Mishnah's order about Shabbat and holidays.

check.q: Why do Hanukkah's rules appear in tractate Shabbat?
choices: because Hanukkah always falls on Shabbat
because the Mishnah has a chapter called Hanukkah
because the discussion began with oils that may be used for Shabbat lamps
check.why: The Gemara on Shabbat 21b was discussing lamp oils and wicks when it turned to Hanukkah.

check.q: In the Talmud's way of counting, an hour is what?
choices: the time to recite the Shema
check.why: Hours are twelfths of daylight, so they change length with the seasons.

lessons.title: The Moves of a Sugya
lessons.mainIdea: Both sugyot in this chapter follow the same pattern of question, proof, objection and answer, which is the pattern of the whole Talmud.
reading: Put the two sugyot side by side. On Berakhot 2a the *question* is: what does the Mishnah assume? The *proof* is Deuteronomy 6:7. The *objection* is: then why evening first? The answer is Genesis 1:5, and the Gemara moves on to test the markers of nightfall against one another. On Shabbat 21b the question is: what is Hanukkah? The proof is a baraita. Then a new question: how many lights? Two views, two reasons, and a ruling that follows Hillel.

These moves have names in the study hall. A question is often introduced with "from where do we know this?" An objection begins "but it was taught." An answer can be "this is not difficult," followed by a distinction between two cases. Learning to spot the moves is the main skill of reading the Talmud in paraphrase, before reading it in the original.

A *chavruta*, a study partner, makes the moves easier to see. One partner reads the question aloud; the other guesses the objection before reading it. The Talmud was written to be argued through, not read silently. Its first page and its Hanukkah page both invite the reader to ask the next question.

words.d: a challenge to a claim in the Gemara, often from a verse or a baraita that seems to disagree
a study partner; Talmud is traditionally studied by two people arguing through a page together

look.title: Label the Moves
look.text: Line 1: Where does the teacher stand? Line 2: On the verse, when you lie down and when you rise up. Line 3: But why teach evening before morning? Line 4: The verse says lie down first; also, there was evening and there was morning. These four lines open the Talmud on Berakhot 2a.
look.prompt: Label each line as question, proof, objection or answer. Then write one more objection a study partner might raise.

check.q: Which is the correct order of the moves in a sugya?
check.why: A sugya opens with a question, brings a proof, faces an objection and gives an answer.

check.q: What is a chavruta?
check.why: A chavruta is a study partner; Talmud is traditionally learned by two people together.

check.q: On Shabbat 21b, what serves as the proof for what Hanukkah is?
choices: a baraita about the jar of oil
check.why: The Gemara answers "What is Hanukkah?" with a baraita, an early teaching about the oil.

review.q: What is the first question in the Mishnah of Berakhot?
choices: From when do we recite the evening Shema?
How many watches are in a night?
review.why: Berakhot 1:1 opens by asking from when the Shema may be recited in the evening.

review.q: Which three views on the latest time for the evening Shema appear in Berakhot 1:1?
choices: first watch, second watch, third watch
review.why: Rabbi Eliezer says the first watch, the Sages say midnight, and Rabban Gamliel says dawn.

choices: a unit of Talmudic argument on one question
one of the six orders of the Mishnah
a priest's share of the harvest
review.why: A sugya is one unit of argument: question, proof, objection, answer.

choices: the thirty-nine categories of Shabbat work
review.why: Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists "forty less one" main categories of forbidden labor.

review.q: What source does the Gemara in Shabbat 49b connect the thirty-nine labors to?
review.why: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama teaches that the categories match the labors of the tabernacle.

review.q: Which of these describes the House of Hillel's way of lighting Hanukkah lamps?
choices: eight lights, going down by one each night
one light, going up by one each night
review.why: The House of Hillel begins with one and adds one each night, because holiness goes up.

review.q: Which of these is true about the books of Maccabees and the Talmud's account of Hanukkah?
choices: only the Talmud mentions the eight days
only the Talmud mentions the jar of oil
the Maccabees books are part of the Talmud
both say the festival lasts seven days
review.why: Both speak of eight days, but the jar of oil appears in the rabbinic account, not in 1 or 2 Maccabees.

review.q: Why did Rabban Gamliel say the Sages set midnight as the limit for the Shema?
choices: the priests finished eating by then
as a fence, to keep people from missing it
the stars can no longer be seen
the first watch ends at midnight
review.why: The midnight limit is a fence around the real limit of dawn, meant to keep people from putting it off.

chapters.title: The Ox, the Pit and the Fire: Damages and Neighbors
chapters.bigQuestion: When one person harms another, what does the Talmud say they owe, and why does it care about more than money?

story.title: A Pit in the Street
story.kicker: A study class in Chicago spends a whole evening on one open hole in the road.
paragraphs: It is a Wednesday night at a synagogue in Skokie, just north of Chicago. Six adults and two teenagers sit at a long table with a volume of tractate Bava Kamma open. The teacher reads the case aloud. A man digs a pit in a public street and leaves it open. An ox wanders by and falls in. Who pays?

"The man who dug it," says one of the teenagers. "Obviously." The teacher nods and turns the page. The Gemara is not done. What if the pit was dug on the man's own land and he gave up the land? What if he covered it, but the cover was weak? What if the ox was blind, or it was night? The questions keep coming.

The class works through them one by one. Some cases seem silly at first, until someone mentions a broken sidewalk near their house. Another person talks about a rake left on a lawn. The old questions start to sound like new ones. Who is responsible for a danger that just waits?

By the end of the night, they have covered part of a page. The teacher smiles. "The Talmud spends pages on this pit," she says. "It is not really about oxen. It is about how we share a street." The class closes the book and agrees to come back next week.
story.think: Why do you think the Talmud asks so many questions about a single open pit? Where in your neighborhood could a "pit" be waiting?

lessons.title: The Mishnah's Four Fathers
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah sorts harm into four main kinds, the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire, and asks who is responsible.
reading: Tractate Bava Kamma, whose name means "the first gate," opens with a list. The Mishnah says there are four *avot nezikin*, four "fathers" or main kinds of damage. They are the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire. Each one comes from a law in the Torah, mostly in Exodus 21 and 22.

Why call them fathers? In the Talmud's language, a father is a main category. Smaller cases that work the same way are its "children." An ox that gores is a father. A goat that butts is like a child of that father. The list helps a judge sort a new case by asking which old case it looks like.

The Gemara then asks what each word really means. The Mishnah's third item is the maveh. Rav, a teacher in Babylonia around 220 CE, says it means the animal's tooth, eating in someone's field. His colleague Shmuel says it means a person who causes harm. The Gemara keeps both views and tests each one. That is how a *sugya* often starts: with the meaning of one word.

words.d: the "fathers of damage"; the four main kinds of harm listed in Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1
one unit of Talmud discussion that moves by question, proof, objection and answer
"the first gate"; the tractate of the Talmud about damages and injuries

look.title: The First Mishnah of Bava Kamma
look.text: There are four main kinds of damage: the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire. They are not all alike. What they share is that each one tends to cause harm, and the one who is responsible for it must pay from the best of his land.
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1, paraphrased in plain English (Danby's translation, 1933, is not public domain)
look.prompt: What do the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire have in common, according to this mishnah?

check.q: What does the Talmud mean by a "father" of damage?
choices: the oldest rabbi who taught about harm
a parent who pays for a child's damage
the owner of the injured animal
check.why: In the Talmud's language a father (av) is a main category; smaller cases like it are its children.

check.q: Which item is NOT one of the four fathers in Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1?
check.why: The Mishnah lists the ox, the pit, the grazing animal (maveh) and the fire. Theft is treated elsewhere.

check.q: How do Rav and Shmuel disagree about the word maveh?
choices: Rav says it is a fire; Shmuel says it is a pit
Both say it is an ox, but disagree about its color
Rav says it is an animal's tooth; Shmuel says it is a person
Rav says it is a thief; Shmuel says it is a flood
check.why: The Gemara on Bava Kamma 3b records Rav reading maveh as the tooth and Shmuel reading it as a person.

lessons.title: The Pit in the Street
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah makes the person who digs and leaves open a pit pay for an animal that falls in, and the rabbis ask what counts as a pit.
reading: Exodus 21:33 describes a man who opens or digs a pit and does not cover it. An ox or a donkey falls in. The Torah says the owner of the pit must pay. The rabbis read this as a lesson about hazards. A danger you create and leave for others is your responsibility.

The Mishnah and Gemara then press on the details. How deep must a pit be to kill an animal? The Mishnah gives ten handbreadths. What if a person digs in the public street, not on their own land? What if they covered it, but badly? What about a stone or a bucket left in the road? The Gemara treats these as children of the pit.

The pit is different from the ox. An ox moves and chooses. A pit just waits. Yet both can hurt a stranger who did nothing wrong. Readers have seen the pit laws as a way of protecting anyone who walks in a shared space. A city sidewalk left with an open hole is a modern pit.

words.d: something left in a place where it can hurt people or animals
in the Talmud, a public space such as a street or market, shared by everyone

look.title: Exodus 21:33–34
look.text: And if a man shall open a pit, or if a man shall dig a pit and not cover it, and an ox or an ass fall therein, the owner of the pit shall make it good; he shall give money unto the owner of them, and the dead beast shall be his.
look.prompt: Who has to pay in this verse, and what does the one who pays get to keep?

check.q: According to Exodus 21:33–34, who pays when an ox falls into an open pit?
choices: nobody, because it was an accident
check.why: The verse says the owner of the pit shall make it good.

check.q: Why do the rabbis treat a stone left in the road like a pit?
choices: It was dug into the ground
It moves on its own like an ox
It is a hazard someone left where it can hurt others
check.why: The Gemara treats obstacles left in public as children of the pit: harms that wait for a victim.

check.q: How is a pit different from an ox as a kind of damage?
choices: A pit is always on private land
A pit stays still, while an ox moves and acts
A pit can never cause harm to people
An ox is not in the Mishnah's list
check.why: The pit is a fixed hazard; the ox is a moving one. Both are fathers of damage.

lessons.title: Fire That Spreads
lessons.mainIdea: Fire is a father of damage because it spreads beyond the one who lit it, so the one who lit it must be careful where it goes.
reading: Exodus 22:5 imagines a fire that catches in thorns and spreads to a neighbor's grain. The Torah says the one who started the fire must pay. The Mishnah lists fire as the fourth father of damage.

Fire is a strange kind of harm. You light it in one place. Wind carries it to another. The Gemara asks whether fire is like your arrows, harm you send out yourself, or like your property, something you own that gets loose. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish take different sides. Each view changes who pays for what.

The Mishnah also asks how far a fire may be from a wall or a field. It asks what happens if a person gave a burning coal to a child who could not be careful. In that case, the Mishnah says, the one who handed it over is exempt under human law but liable under the laws of Heaven. Readers see a lesson here. Some duties go beyond what a court can enforce.

words.d: responsible to pay for a harm under the law
free from having to pay under the law of the court

look.title: The Coal and the Child
look.text: Maya hands a lit barbecue lighter to her little cousin, who is six. The cousin sets a pile of leaves on fire, and it burns a neighbor's fence. Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:4 discusses a case like this, with a burning coal given to a child.
look.prompt: Who should pay for the fence? Why might the Mishnah say a court cannot make Maya pay, but she is still responsible in a deeper way?

check.q: Where does the Torah describe a fire that spreads to a neighbor's grain?
check.why: Exodus 22:5 (in the JPS numbering) is the verse on fire spreading to a neighbor's field.

check.q: What does "liable" mean?
choices: responsible to pay under the law
check.why: Liable means responsible to pay. Exempt is the opposite.

check.q: What question does the Gemara ask about fire?
choices: Is it one of the 39 labors of Shabbat?
Should it be lit on Hanukkah?
Is it like a person's arrows or like a person's property?
Was it created on the first day?
check.why: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish debate whether fire is like one's arrows or one's property, and the answer affects who pays.

lessons.title: The Innocent Ox and the Warned Ox
lessons.mainIdea: An ox with no history of goring pays half the damage, while an ox known to gore pays full damage, because its owner was warned.
reading: Exodus 21:28–36 describes an ox that gores. The Torah treats two cases differently. In one, the ox has never gored before. In the other, the ox has gored before and the owner was warned, but did not guard it.

The Mishnah gives these two cases names. An ox with no record is *tam*, which means "innocent" or "simple." An ox that has gored three times, with the owner warned, becomes *mu'ad*, "warned" or "forewarned." For damage to other animals, a tam ox's owner pays half the damage, and only from the ox's own value. A mu'ad ox's owner pays in full.

Why the difference? The owner of a tam ox could not easily know. The owner of a mu'ad ox had been told and did nothing. The rule weighs what the owner could have known. It protects the victim, and it also is fair to an owner who was surprised. Many readers compare it to modern rules about a dog known to bite.

words.d: "innocent"; an ox with no record of goring, whose owner pays half the damage
"warned"; an ox known to gore, whose owner was warned and pays full damage

look.title: What the Owner Pays
rows: Grazing animal in a neighbor's field
look.prompt: Which case pays only half? What is different about that case?

check.q: What does tam mean when the Mishnah uses it for an ox?
choices: an ox that has gored three times
an ox that belongs to the Temple
an ox that fell into a pit
an ox with no record of goring
check.why: Tam means innocent or simple: an ox with no history of goring.

check.q: When does an ox become mu'ad?
choices: after it has gored three times and the owner was warned
as soon as it is born
when it is sold to a new owner
when it grazes in someone's field
check.why: The Mishnah says an ox becomes mu'ad after goring three times with the owner warned.

check.q: Why does the owner of a mu'ad ox pay more?
choices: The owner was warned and did not guard the ox
The Torah forbids owning a mu'ad ox
check.why: The rule weighs what the owner knew; the mu'ad owner had been warned.

lessons.title: An Eye for an Eye
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud reads "an eye for an eye" as a rule about paying the value of the injury, not about harming the one who injured.
reading: Exodus 21:24 says, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." Read alone, it sounds like a rule of revenge. The Mishnah and the Gemara read it another way. They hold that it means the one who injures must pay money for the value of what was lost.

The Gemara on Bava Kamma 83b–84a argues for this reading. It asks: what if a blind man blinds someone? What if a person with weak eyes blinds a person with strong ones? Taking an eye back could never be equal. It also points to a verse that says a court may not take money in place of a life for a murderer, and argues that for injuries money may be taken. Several rabbis bring several proofs.

Rabbinic tradition holds that the money reading was how the verse was always meant. Many modern historians say the reading grew over time. Either way, Jewish law as the Talmud develops it did not take eyes. It measured the harm and paid for it. Readers have seen mercy in that move, for both the victim and the one at fault.

words.d: the part of the Talmud that discusses and argues about the Mishnah
money paid to make up for a loss or injury

look.title: Exodus 21:23–25
look.text: But if any harm follow, then thou shalt give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
look.prompt: The Gemara reads this verse as a rule about money. What problems with a literal reading does it point to?

check.q: How does the Talmud read "eye for an eye"?
choices: as paying money for the value of the injury
as a command to harm the one who injured
as a story about the Temple
as a rule only for oxen
check.why: The Mishnah and Gemara (Bava Kamma 83b–84a) read the verse as a rule of monetary compensation.

check.q: Which question does the Gemara ask to show a literal reading will not work?
choices: What time is the evening Shema?
Who owns a cloak found in the street?
How deep must a pit be?
What if a blind person blinds someone?
check.why: The Gemara asks how a blind person could "give an eye," showing a literal rule could never be equal.

check.q: How do many modern historians describe the money reading?
choices: as a mistake the rabbis never made
as a rule from the Hanukkah story
as a reading that developed over time
as the view of Shmuel alone
check.why: Rabbinic tradition holds the money reading was always meant; many historians see it as developing over time.

lessons.title: Five Payments for an Injury
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah says a person who injures another pays for five things: the damage, the pain, the healing, lost work and the shame.
reading: Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1 lists what a person who injures another must pay. There are five parts. The damage is the lasting loss. The pain is the suffering. The healing is the doctor's cost. The lost work is the time the person could not earn. The last is *boshet*, the shame or embarrassment.

The list is careful. The Mishnah does not stop at the body. It counts the hours of work lost and the feeling of being shamed. A person hurt in front of others may carry that hurt longer than a bruise. The Mishnah even says the payment for shame depends on who shamed and who was shamed.

This is where the Talmud's argument and its mercy meet. The rules ask a court to look at the whole person. Readers today compare the list to modern injury law, which also pays for medical bills, lost wages and pain. The Talmud's list adds shame, and treats a person's dignity as something that can be harmed.

words.d: shame or embarrassment; one of the five payments for an injury in Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1
the worth and respect every person deserves

look.title: Counting the Harm
look.text: In gym class, Jordan trips another student on purpose. The student sprains an ankle, misses a week of a paid after-school job, needs a doctor, is in pain, and everyone laughed when it happened. Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1 names five things the one who injures must pay for.
look.prompt: Match each part of the story to one of the five payments. Which one would a modern court be least likely to count?

check.q: How many payments does Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1 list for an injury?
check.why: The Mishnah lists five: damage, pain, healing, lost work and shame.

check.q: What is boshet?
check.why: Boshet is shame, the fifth payment in Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1.

check.q: What does the list show about how the Mishnah sees an injury?
choices: It counts harm to a person's dignity, not only the body
It lets the injured person take revenge
It leaves the matter to the injured person's family
check.why: By including pain, lost work and shame, the Mishnah looks at the whole person.

lessons.title: Two Hold a Cloak
lessons.mainIdea: When two people both grab a found cloak and each claims it, the Mishnah has each swear and they divide it.
reading: Tractate Bava Metzia, "the middle gate," opens with a famous case. Two people hold one cloak. One says, "I found it. It is all mine." The other says the same. No one saw who picked it up first. What should a court do?

The Mishnah on Bava Metzia 2a answers: each one swears an oath that they own no less than half, and they split it. Then it changes the case. What if one says "It is all mine" and the other says "Half is mine"? The second person already agrees that half belongs to the first. Only the other half is in dispute. So the first gets three quarters and the second one quarter.

The Gemara spends many pages on this mishnah. Why an oath? Why not let whoever is stronger keep it? The rabbis worry that a person might grab what is not theirs. The oath asks each person to face the truth. The split protects both from losing everything when no one can know for certain.

words.d: "the middle gate"; the tractate about found objects, loans, work and fair dealing
a serious promise, made before a court, that what you say is true

look.title: Dividing the Cloak
look.prompt: Why does the person who claims only half get one quarter, not one half?

check.q: What does each person do before the cloak is divided?
choices: swears an oath that they own at least half
pays a fine to the court
tells the story to a priest
waits for the owner for a year
check.why: The Mishnah (Bava Metzia 2a) has each swear that they own no less than half.

check.q: If one says "all mine" and the other says "half mine," how is it split?
check.why: The second already agrees half is the first's, so only half is in dispute and it is split.

check.q: What does the name Bava Metzia mean?
check.why: Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia and Bava Batra are the first, middle and last gates.

lessons.title: Lost Objects and Giving Up Hope
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah tells a finder to return lost things, and the rabbis ask when an owner has given up hope, which the Talmud calls ye'ush.
reading: Deuteronomy 22:1–3 tells a person who finds a neighbor's lost animal or garment to return it. It ends with a strong line: you may not look away. The rabbis read this as a *mitzvah*, a commandment, called returning lost objects.

The Mishnah on Bava Metzia 2:1 lists things a finder may keep, such as scattered fruit or coins with no mark. Why? The owner cannot identify them and has surely given up hope. The Talmud calls giving up hope *ye'ush*, "despair." Once an owner despairs, the object may belong to the finder. If an item has a mark, like a knot or a name, the finder must announce it.

The Gemara asks a hard question. What if the owner does not know yet that the thing is lost? Abaye and Rava, teachers in Babylonia around 330 CE, disagree. Most of the Gemara's long discussion follows from their debate. The rules try to protect the owner's hope while being fair to an honest finder.

words.d: a commandment; in Jewish tradition, a duty from the Torah
"despair"; when an owner gives up hope of getting a lost thing back
a sign or mark that lets an owner identify a lost object

look.title: Deuteronomy 22:3
look.text: You must do the same with your neighbor's donkey, his garment, and anything else he has lost that you find. You may not hide yourself from it.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 22:3, paraphrased from the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: What do you think "you may not hide yourself" means for a finder?

check.q: What does ye'ush mean?
choices: a sign or mark on an object
an owner giving up hope of getting a lost thing back
check.why: Ye'ush is despair; once the owner despairs, a finder may keep an unmarked object.

check.q: Why may a finder keep scattered coins with no mark?
choices: The owner cannot identify them and has surely given up hope
The Torah says all coins go to the finder
Coins are one of the four fathers of damage
check.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 2:1 lets a finder keep unmarked things because the owner has no sign and has despaired.

check.q: Which pair of rabbis disagrees about an owner who does not yet know a thing is lost?
choices: Rav and Shmuel on the maveh
check.why: The debate on unaware despair in Bava Metzia is between Abaye and Rava.

lessons.title: Wronging With Words
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah teaches that hurting someone with words is a real wrong, which it calls ona'at devarim.
reading: Leviticus 25:17 says, in plain words, do not wrong one another. The Mishnah reads it as a rule about speech. It calls this *ona'at devarim*, "wronging with words." A person can be cheated with money. A person can also be hurt with a sentence.

Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 gives examples. Do not remind a person who has changed their ways about what they used to do. Do not remind a convert's child of the deeds of their ancestors. Do not ask a seller the price of something if you have no plan to buy it. Each example protects someone from shame or false hope.

The Gemara on Bava Metzia 58b adds a sharp teaching. Shaming someone in public is compared to shedding blood, because the face goes pale. The rabbis say that wronging with words is in some ways worse than cheating with money. Money can be paid back. Words can not be taken back in the same way.

words.d: "wronging with words"; hurting or shaming a person through speech
the first written collection of rabbinic teaching, edited around 200 CE

look.title: The Group Chat
look.text: A student in your class had a hard year and now works hard and is kind to everyone. In a group chat, someone posts, "Remember what she did in fourth grade?" Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 says not to remind a person who has changed of what they used to do.
look.prompt: Why might the Mishnah treat this as a real wrong, even though nothing was stolen? What could someone in the chat do instead?

check.q: What does ona'at devarim mean?
check.why: Ona'at devarim is hurting someone through speech, taught in Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10.

check.q: Which is an example from Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10?
choices: leaving a pit open in the street
letting an ox graze in a field
asking a seller a price when you do not plan to buy
check.why: The Mishnah lists asking a price with no plan to buy as a way of wronging with words.

check.q: Why does the Gemara compare public shaming to shedding blood?
choices: Because shaming is one of the 39 labors
Because it is done with a knife
Because the shamed person's face goes pale
Because the Torah says so in Exodus 21
check.why: Bava Metzia 58b says the face of the shamed person loses its color, as if blood were shed.

lessons.title: Love Your Neighbor
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Akiva called "love your neighbor as yourself" a great principle of the Torah, and other rabbis offered other great principles.
reading: Leviticus 19:18 says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Rabbinic tradition reports that Rabbi Akiva, a teacher of the early second century, called this verse a great principle of the Torah. His colleague Ben Azzai named a different verse: the one saying that humans are made in the likeness of God.

The Talmud tells another famous story about Hillel on Shabbat 31a. A man asks Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel answers: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it.

These teachings link the damage laws to something larger. The ox, the pit, the lost cloak and the cruel word are all about neighbors. Readers have long seen the laws of Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia as the details of this principle. Different Jewish movements read the principle in different ways, but many point to it.

words.d: a big idea that many smaller rules come from
in the Torah, a fellow person; the rabbis discuss how widely the word reaches

look.title: Leviticus 19:18
look.text: Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
look.prompt: The verse forbids two things before it gives the command to love. What are they, and why might they come first?

check.q: Who called "love your neighbor as yourself" a great principle of the Torah?
check.why: Rabbinic tradition reports Rabbi Akiva calling Leviticus 19:18 a great principle.

check.q: What did Hillel say when asked to teach the Torah on one foot?
choices: From when do we recite the evening Shema?
There are four fathers of damage
Each one swears and they divide it
What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor
check.why: Shabbat 31a tells how Hillel summed up the Torah this way, then said to go and learn.

check.q: What verse did Ben Azzai name as a great principle?
choices: the verse about the evening Shema
the verse saying humans are made in the likeness of God
the verse about a pit left open
check.why: Ben Azzai pointed to the verse on human beings made in God's likeness, a principle for all people.

lessons.title: The Porters' Wages
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells of a judge who told a rich man to pay poor workers even after they broke his barrels, beyond what the strict law required.
reading: Leviticus 19:13 says a worker's wages must not stay with the employer overnight. The rabbis read this as a rule to pay workers on time. A worker who lives day to day needs the money now. The Mishnah and Gemara on Bava Metzia work out when and how wages must be paid.

Bava Metzia 83a tells a story. Some porters broke a barrel of wine while carrying it for Rabbah bar bar Hanan. He took their cloaks to cover his loss. They went to Rav. Rav told him to give back their cloaks. The porters said they were poor, had worked all day and were hungry. Rav told him to pay their wages too.

Rabbah asked, "Is that the law?" Rav answered, "Yes," and quoted Proverbs 2:20 about walking in the way of good people. Readers call this going *lifnim mishurat hadin*, beyond the line of the law. The story shows a judge weighing the poor worker's need, not only the strict rules.

words.d: the pay a worker earns for a day's or a week's work
"inside the line of the law"; doing more than the strict law requires, out of fairness or kindness

look.title: The Broken Barrel
look.text: Two porters carry a barrel of wine and break it. The owner takes their cloaks. A judge tells him to return the cloaks and then to pay them, because they are poor and worked all day (Bava Metzia 83a).
look.prompt: Was the judge fair to the owner? Give one reason for the owner's side and one for the porters' side.

check.q: What does Leviticus 19:13 say about a worker's wages?
choices: They must not stay with the employer overnight
They should be paid once a year
They are paid only if nothing is broken
They go to the Temple first
check.why: Leviticus 19:13 says a hired worker's wages must not stay with the employer until morning.

check.q: In Bava Metzia 83a, what did Rav tell Rabbah bar bar Hanan to do?
choices: keep the cloaks and fire the porters
return the porters' cloaks and pay their wages
check.why: Rav ordered the cloaks returned and the wages paid, citing Proverbs 2:20.

check.q: What does lifnim mishurat hadin mean?
choices: doing more than the strict law requires
check.why: It means acting beyond the line of the law, as Rav asks in the porters' story.

review.q: Which tractate opens with the four fathers of damage?
review.why: Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1 lists the ox, the pit, the grazing animal and the fire.

review.q: An ox has gored three times and its owner was warned. What is it called?
review.why: Mu'ad means warned; its owner pays full damage.

review.q: How does the Gemara on Bava Kamma 84a read "eye for an eye"?
choices: as a rule for oxen only
as payment of money for the injury
as a command to blind the one at fault
review.why: The Talmud reads the verse as monetary compensation, with several proofs.

review.q: Which is one of the five payments in Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1?
review.why: The five are damage, pain, healing, lost work and shame (boshet).

review.q: In the case of the two who hold a cloak, what happens when both say "it is all mine"?
choices: It is given to the Temple
Each swears and they split it in half
review.why: Bava Metzia 2a: each swears to owning no less than half, and they divide.

review.q: Which idea explains why a finder may keep unmarked coins?
review.why: Once the owner has despaired of an item with no sign, the finder may keep it.

review.q: What teaching about speech does Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 give?
choices: Do not remind a person who has changed of their past deeds
Light one more candle each night
Pay half damage for a tam ox
review.why: This is an example of ona'at devarim, wronging with words.

review.q: Why is the porters' story on Bava Metzia 83a a story of mercy?
choices: The barrel is repaired by a miracle
The judge asks the owner to pay poor workers beyond the strict law
review.why: Rav cites Proverbs 2:20 and has the owner act beyond the line of the law.
